answer.evidence: The pole shaft (width 6-7, rows 31-42) is a plain vertical face. The crossarm at rows 5-12 is a horizontal beam seen face-on. It has only a 1-row highlight at row 7 and 4 rows of flat face below, with no ellipse or lid plate overhanging the shaft. The transformer can shows a lighter lid at rows 17-20, but it is a side attachment, not the main body. The top end is two small insulator caps (rows 0-4), not an elliptical cap plate, so the top reads as at most a 2-row rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin pole with a transformer can and a pale cap. It measures 25 visible tones per 16x16 tile, above the well (20) and cheese stall (17). Near-flat coverage is 0% and none of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines carry a colour tint (dark brown beside the wood, dark grey-blue beside the can) rather than a black sticker line. By eye, the pole has a lit and a shaded side with grain, and the transformer can has several grey steps with highlight and shadow. The cap and cross-arm hardware are shaded with a few steps instead of one flat fill. It is a sparse, thin object, but it does not look flatter or thinner than the lamp-crook and bench references, so it should sit acceptably beside them.

answer.evidence: The main body is a thin wooden pole, 6 px wide at rows 37-42. Its top end is a crossarm, rows 5-13, with a width profile of 11, 12, 14, 12, 11. It is drawn face-on as a beam with one light edge line at row 7 and dark shading at rows 11-12. It has no back rim and no front rim, so it is not an ellipse plate; it reads as a vertical beam with rounded ends, so I set rounded_at_both_edges to false. The small white insulators at rows 0-4 are ornaments. The grey transformer can at rows 17-29 has a pale lid at rows 17-21, but it is a side-mounted attachment, not the cap of the shaft. The pole itself shows no overhanging top plate, so the object reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin pole prop, so I judged it mostly by eye against the lamp, well and stall references. It has about 25 visible tones per full tile, which is above the stall (17) and well (20) references. Near-flat coverage is 0% and none of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is tinted. Edges are dark brown next to the wood and dark grey-blue next to the transformer can, not a uniform black sticker line. The pole has grain, the can has banded highlight and shadow, and the base has a striped band. The snow cap is shaded in several steps rather than drawn as one flat white. Shading depth is about 5 steps on the wood and can, close to the references' 5-6. It is not noticeably thinner or flatter than the lamp-crook next to it, and it matches the stall and well on tone density.

The transformer canister (rows 17-30) is drawn as a front-facing cylinder with no visible lid ellipse. The white insulator tips at rows 0-4 are small decor on the crossarm. The silhouette widens to 14 and narrows again, but this is the outline of a flat beam, not a horizontal cap plate seen from above. The result is a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tall, thin pole prop with a transformer can and a pale cap, comparable in kind to the lamp-crook and stall references. On the primary facts it matches or beats the references: 25 visible tones per tile against 17-20 for the stall and well, and 0% near-flat coverage. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, with dark brown beside the wood and a dark grey-blue lean beside the can, rather than a uniform black sticker line. By eye, the pole has grain and several brown steps, and the transformer can has highlight, mid and shadow bands plus small fittings. It is a thin object, so I judge density by eye. It does not look thinner or flatter than the references and shows no large flat fills. Texture is a little less rich than the stall or well, but it is acceptable beside them.
